content.html:
Module 4›Chapter 4.2›eBGP Configuration Fundamentals on Junos
Overview

Starting eBGP on Junos

eBGP is the first step for inter-AS connectivity, allowing your network to exchange routes with external partners or the global internet.

  • •Primarily configured within the [edit protocols bgp] hierarchy.
  • •Connects routers in different Autonomous Systems.
  • •Establishes a TCP session on port 179 with the remote neighbor.
Key Parameters

Core eBGP Configuration Elements

Local AS Number

Your router's unique Autonomous System identifier.

Remote Neighbor IP

The IP address of the peer router in the external AS.

Remote AS Number

The Autonomous System identifier of the peer network.

Interface IP

The local interface IP used for peering.

Scenario Example

Router A (AS 64500, IP 192.168.1.1) wants to peer with Router B (AS 65000, IP 192.168.1.2).

Key Takeaway

Correctly defining local AS, remote IP, and remote AS is non-negotiable for eBGP session establishment.

screens.title: Defining Local AS and BGP Group
screens.narratorSegment: The first step in configuring eBGP on a Junos device is to define your router's local Autonomous System number. This is a global setting that tells BGP which AS your router belongs to. You achieve this using the set routing-options autonomous-system command, followed by your AS number. For instance, if your router is in AS 64500, you would use set routing-options autonomous-system 64500. This command is crucial because it establishes your router's identity within the BGP routing domain. Next, we create a BGP group. BGP groups are a powerful Junos feature that allows you to apply common configuration parameters to multiple neighbors, simplifying management and ensuring consistency. We name our group, for example, EBGP-PEER, and then specify type external to explicitly indicate that this group is for eBGP peering. This distinction is important as it influences how BGP behaves, particularly regarding default Time To Live values and direct connection requirements. Without defining the local AS, BGP cannot operate, and without a group, you'd have to configure each neighbor individually, which can become cumbersome in larger deployments. Defining Local AS and BGP Group means the local as defines identity, while bgp groups streamline ebgp neighbor configurations.. In practical terms, setting your router's identity and organizing bgp neighbors.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4›Chapter 4.2›Defining Local AS and BGP Group
Junos CLI Configuration
set routing-options autonomous-system 64500
set protocols bgp group EBGP-PEER type external
Command Breakdown

routing-options autonomous-system: Defines the local AS number for the router. This is a global BGP setting.

Explanation

Understanding Each Command

  • •Local AS Number: Establishes your router's identity for BGP. All BGP sessions on this router will use this AS.
  • •BGP Group: A logical container for neighbors sharing common parameters. Simplifies configuration and management.
  • •type external: Explicitly marks the group for eBGP peering, influencing default behaviors like TTL.
Example Scenario

Router A (AS 64500) sets its local AS and creates an eBGP group named 'EBGP-PEER' to connect to an external network.

Key Takeaway

The local AS is a global BGP identifier, and BGP groups are essential for organizing and applying consistent configurations to eBGP neighbors.

screens.title: Configuring the eBGP Neighbor
screens.narratorSegment: Once you've defined your local Autonomous System and created an eBGP group, the next critical step is to specify the remote BGP neighbor. This involves telling your Junos router exactly who it needs to peer with. You do this using the set protocols bgp group neighbor peer-as command. The refers to the BGP group you just created, for example, EBGP-PEER. The is the IP address of the remote router's interface that will be used for the BGP session. Finally, the peer-as specifies the Autonomous System number of that remote neighbor. This peer-as value must precisely match the actual AS number configured on the remote router. A common mistake here is a mismatch in the peer-as value, which will prevent the BGP session from ever establishing, often resulting in the local router being stuck in an 'Active' state as it repeatedly tries to connect but receives incorrect BGP Open messages. After committing these changes, your Junos router will attempt to establish a TCP connection on port 179 with the specified neighbor, initiating the eBGP peering process. This command is the heart of eBGP connectivity, linking your AS to an external one.

keyIdea.title: Neighbor Definition
keyIdea.text: Accurately defining the remote neighbor's IP and AS is crucial for eBGP session establishment.

content.html:
Module 4›Chapter 4.2›Configuring the eBGP Neighbor
Junos CLI Configuration
set protocols bgp group EBGP-PEER neighbor 192.168.1.2 peer-as 65000
Command Breakdown

neighbor <IP> peer-as <ASN>: Defines the remote BGP neighbor's IP address and its Autonomous System Number.

Explanation

Key Elements of Neighbor Configuration

  • •Neighbor IP Address: The specific IP of the remote router's interface for peering.
  • •Peer AS Number: The AS number of the remote network. Must match exactly for session establishment.
  • •TCP Port 179: BGP uses TCP port 179 for session establishment.
Common Mistake

A mismatch in the peer-as value will prevent the BGP session from forming, often leaving the session in an 'Active' state.

Key Takeaway

The neighbor command with the correct peer-as is the final piece to initiate eBGP peering and inter-AS route exchange.

screens.title: Verifying eBGP Session Status
screens.narratorSegment: After configuring your eBGP session, verification is absolutely critical to ensure everything is working as expected. You need to confirm that the BGP session has successfully established and that your router is actively exchanging routes with its peer. The show bgp summary command is your go-to for a quick overview. It provides a concise summary of all BGP groups and neighbors, indicating their current state. You'll want to see the state as 'Established', which means the BGP session is fully operational and ready to exchange routing information. If you see states like 'Active' or 'Idle', it indicates a problem that needs troubleshooting. For more detailed information about a specific BGP session, you can use show bgp neighbor. This command provides extensive details, including the session's state, the number of messages sent and received, and any error counters. This level of detail is invaluable for diagnosing issues, such as why a session might be stuck in an 'Active' state, which often points to a peer-as mismatch or connectivity problem. Regularly checking these commands is a fundamental practice for any network engineer managing BGP.

keyIdea.title: Session Health Check
keyIdea.text: `show bgp summary` and `show bgp neighbor` are essential for monitoring eBGP session status.

content.html:
Module 4›Chapter 4.2›Verifying eBGP Session Status
Junos CLI Verification
show bgp summary
show bgp neighbor 192.168.1.2
Expected Output (Summary)

Look for 'Established' state under the 'State' column for your eBGP neighbor.

Explanation

Interpreting BGP Status

  • •show bgp summary: Provides a high-level overview of all BGP groups and neighbors.
  • •'Established' State: Indicates a healthy, operational BGP session.
  • •'Active' / 'Idle' States: Signal issues preventing session establishment, requiring troubleshooting.
  • •show bgp neighbor: Offers granular details for a specific peer, including message counts and error logs.
Key Takeaway

Regularly using show bgp summary and show bgp neighbor is crucial for confirming eBGP session health and for initial troubleshooting.

screens.title: Verifying Learned Routes
screens.narratorSegment: Beyond just verifying the BGP session status, it's equally important to confirm that your router is actually learning routes from its eBGP peer and installing them into its routing table. The command show route protocol bgp is specifically designed for this purpose. This command filters the routing table to display only those routes that have been learned via the BGP protocol. When you execute this command, you should see prefixes advertised by your eBGP neighbor, indicating a successful route exchange. If the BGP session is 'Established' but you don't see any expected routes, it could point to an issue with routing policies on either your router or the peer, or perhaps the peer isn't advertising any routes. For example, if your peer is advertising a network like 10.0.0.0/24, you should see an entry for this prefix with BGP as the protocol. This verification step is crucial because a BGP session, while established, is only truly useful if it's facilitating the exchange of reachability information. Without learned routes, your router cannot forward traffic to destinations within the remote Autonomous System, effectively rendering the peering useless for data plane connectivity. Always check for learned routes after establishing a session.

keyIdea.title: Route Table Insight
keyIdea.text: `show route protocol bgp` confirms successful route exchange and installation from eBGP peers.

content.html:
Module 4›Chapter 4.2›Verifying Learned Routes
Junos CLI Verification
show route protocol bgp
Expected Output (Example)

10.0.0.0/24 *[BGP/170] 00:01:23, localpref 100, from 192.168.1.2

Explanation

Interpreting Learned Routes

  • •Purpose: Confirms that routes are being received from the eBGP peer and installed into the local routing table.
  • •Filtering: The command specifically shows routes learned via the BGP protocol.
  • •Troubleshooting: If no routes appear, investigate routing policies on both sides or verify the peer is advertising routes.
Why it Matters

Without learned routes, the eBGP session cannot facilitate data plane connectivity to the remote AS, making it functionally useless.

Key Takeaway

Always verify learned routes with show route protocol bgp to ensure actual inter-AS reachability, not just session establishment.

screens.title: Understanding eBGP Direct Connection
screens.narratorSegment: A common point of confusion and a frequent cause of eBGP peering issues relates to the direct connection requirement. By default, eBGP neighbors are expected to be directly connected, meaning they share a common subnet and can reach each other without an intermediate router. Junos, like other vendors, enforces this check. If your eBGP peers are not directly connected, or if you're peering to a loopback interface – which is a best practice for stability even with eBGP, but requires an Interior Gateway Protocol for reachability – you will encounter problems. The BGP session will likely fail to establish. To overcome this default behavior when peers are not directly connected, you need to use the multihop option. This command effectively disables the direct connection check, allowing the BGP session to form over multiple hops. For example, if Router A and Router B are separated by Router C, you would need multihop configured on both A and B. Failing to configure multihop in such scenarios is a classic troubleshooting challenge, as the session will remain in an 'Active' or 'Idle' state, indicating a connectivity or parameter mismatch issue. Understanding this default behavior is key to successful eBGP deployments in various network topologies.

keyIdea.title: Direct Connection Default
keyIdea.text: eBGP peers are assumed to be directly connected; `multihop` is needed for indirect connections.

content.html:
Module 4›Chapter 4.2›Understanding eBGP Direct Connection
Core Principle

eBGP Direct Connection Requirement

  • •By default, eBGP neighbors must be directly connected (share a common subnet).
  • •This is a security and sanity check to prevent accidental peering.
  • •Peering to loopback interfaces (a best practice) also requires bypassing this check.
Common Issue

Session fails to establish if peers are not directly connected and multihop is not configured.

Junos CLI Solution
set protocols bgp group EBGP-PEER multihop
Command Explanation

The multihop option disables the direct connection check, allowing eBGP sessions to form over multiple network hops.

Key Takeaway

Always consider the physical or logical connectivity between eBGP peers; use multihop when they are not directly connected.

screens.title: Adjusting TTL for Multi-hop eBGP
screens.narratorSegment: Closely related to the multihop option is the concept of Time To Live, or TTL. The TTL field in an IP header limits the lifespan of a packet, decrementing by one at each hop. For directly connected eBGP peers, the default TTL value is typically set to one. This means the BGP Open message, which initiates the session, will only survive one hop, reaching the directly connected neighbor but no further. This default behavior reinforces the direct connection requirement. However, when you configure multihop because your eBGP peers are not directly connected, the default TTL of one becomes insufficient. The BGP Open message would expire before reaching the remote peer. TTL Fundamentals

Time To Live in eBGP

  • •TTL limits packet lifespan, decrementing at each hop.
  • •Default eBGP TTL is 1 for directly connected peers.

Issue with Multihop

If multihop is enabled but TTL is still 1, BGP packets will expire before reaching the remote peer.

Junos CLI Solution
set protocols bgp group EBGP-PEER ttl 255

Manually setting a higher TTL (e.g., 255) ensures BGP packets can traverse multiple hops to reach non-directly connected peers.

For multihop eBGP, ensure TTL is sufficient for packets to reach the peer, either implicitly via multihop or explicitly set.

screens.title: Introduction to BGP Route Policies
screens.narratorSegment: While establishing a basic eBGP session allows for route exchange, you rarely want to accept or advertise *all* routes without any control. This is where Junos policy statements become indispensable. Policy statements are powerful configuration constructs that allow you to define specific criteria and actions for routing policies. They provide granular control over which routes are advertised from your router to a neighbor, known as an export policy, and which routes are accepted from a neighbor into your router's routing table, known as an import policy. For example, you might want to only advertise your specific public IP prefixes to an upstream ISP, preventing accidental route leaks of your internal networks. Conversely, you might want to filter out certain prefixes from a peer to avoid receiving undesirable routes. Policies are essential for security, preventing accidental route leaks, and implementing traffic engineering. Without them, your router could become a conduit for unwanted or incorrect routing information, potentially causing significant network disruptions. Understanding the distinction between import and export policies is fundamental to effective BGP management. Module 4›Chapter 4.2›Introduction to BGP Route Policies
Why Use Policies?

Controlling Route Exchange

  • •Prevent accidental route leaks to external networks.
  • •Filter unwanted or incorrect routes from peers.
  • •Implement traffic engineering strategies.
  • •Enhance network security and stability.
Policy Types

Import vs. Export Policies

Export Policy

Controls routes advertised from your router to the neighbor.

Import Policy

Controls routes accepted from the neighbor into your router's routing table.

Key Takeaway

BGP policies are vital for granular control over route exchange, ensuring security and preventing routing disruptions.

screens.title: Implementing Basic Export Policy
screens.narratorSegment: Let's look at a practical example of implementing a basic export policy on Junos. Suppose you want to advertise only a specific network prefix, for instance, 10.0.0.0 slash 24, to your eBGP peer, and no other internal routes. This is a common requirement for security and control. First, you define a policy statement using set policy-options policy-statement ADVERTISE-MY-PREFIX. Within this policy, you create a term, for example, term 1, and specify the criteria for matching routes. Here, we use from route-filter 10.0.0.0 slash 24 exact to precisely match only that specific prefix. The exact keyword is crucial, as it prevents matching longer or shorter prefixes within that range. Then, you define the action for matching routes, which in this case is then accept. This means any route matching the filter will be accepted for advertisement. Finally, you apply this policy to your eBGP group using the export keyword: set protocols bgp group EBGP-PEER export ADVERTISE-MY-PREFIX. This tells BGP to use this policy when deciding which routes to send out to that specific neighbor. It's important to remember that policies are processed sequentially, and the first match determines the action. Always test your policies in a lab environment before deploying them in production, as incorrect policies can lead to significant routing disruptions or unintended route advertisements.

Module 4›Chapter 4.2›Implementing Basic Export Policy
Junos CLI Configuration
set policy-options policy-statement ADVERTISE-MY-PREFIX term 1 from route-filter 10.0.0.0/24 exact
set policy-options policy-statement ADVERTISE-MY-PREFIX term 1 then accept
set protocols bgp group EBGP-PEER export ADVERTISE-MY-PREFIX
Command Breakdown

Defines a policy to accept only the 10.0.0.0/24 prefix for advertisement and applies it as an export policy.

Explanation

Policy Statement Components

  • •Policy Statement: A named container for routing policy rules.
  • •Term: A logical block within a policy, processed sequentially.
  • •from route-filter: Specifies criteria for matching routes (e.g., prefix, length).
  • •exact: Ensures an exact prefix match, preventing broader or narrower matches.
  • •then accept: The action to take if a route matches the criteria.
Key Takeaway

Export policies are crucial for controlling advertised routes, using route-filter with exact for precise prefix matching.

The first step in configuring eBGP on a Junos device is to define your router's local Autonomous System number. This is a global setting that tells BGP which AS your router belongs to. You achieve this using the set routing-options autonomous-system command, followed by your AS number. For instance, if your router is in AS 64500, you would use set routing-options autonomous-system 64500. This command is crucial because it establishes your router's identity within the BGP routing domain. Next, we create a BGP group. BGP groups are a powerful Junos feature that allows you to apply common configuration parameters to multiple neighbors, simplifying management and ensuring consistency. We name our group, for example, EBGP-PEER, and then specify type external to explicitly indicate that this group is for eBGP peering. This distinction is important as it influences how BGP behaves, particularly regarding default Time To Live values and direct connection requirements. Once you've defined your local Autonomous System and created an eBGP group, the next critical step is to specify the remote BGP neighbor.
